biography.name: Marisol Vega

background.family: Lives with her mother, stepfather, and two younger brothers; relatives nearby exchange rides and childcare.
background.finances: Money covers basics unevenly. She wants an adulthood with substantial income and a house where appliances get replaced immediately.
background.geography: A small town outside Uvalde, Texas, with long drives between school, stores, and relatives.
background.cultureLanguages: English at school and a mixture of Spanish and English with family; she understands more Spanish than she likes speaking publicly.
background.school: A small public high school with shared activity spaces and occasional combined club meetings.
background.accessOpportunities: School activities are the main organized options. Neither parent attended college, and application procedures are unfamiliar to the household.

timeline.story: Marisol spent afternoons sorting bottle caps while her mother folded laundry. She enjoyed choosing which cousin got which color and argued over whether the scratched ones counted. At kindergarten she followed another child's pretend restaurant game, but quickly lost interest when everyone had to draw menus.

She became absorbed in jump rope and wanted a longer turn than the playground rule allowed. She offered to keep count for other children in exchange. Her grandmother liked her elaborate explanations, while her teacher repeatedly asked her to let a quiet classmate finish speaking.

During a family yard sale she asked shoppers what they wanted to spend and bundled mismatched cups together. She remembers getting someone to take the whole box. Later she misplaced the envelope holding several dollars and was banned from collecting money for the rest of that afternoon.

She joined a dance group because two friends attended. Practices felt repetitive, and she quit midway through the year despite enjoying the performance clothes. For a class snack sale, she eagerly discussed prices with adults but left her assigned poster unfinished until another student took it home.

Her brothers began needing someone at home after school. Marisol missed several club meetings and resented hearing decisions afterward. At a weekend fundraiser she persuaded a supplier to lower the price of paper bowls, then annoyed the organizer by promising buyers extra portions without checking the available food.

She liked asking local families to buy raffle tickets because each conversation went differently. A neighbor explained why another request felt burdensome, and she stopped returning to that house. Her grades varied: she remembered spoken discussions easily but rushed written explanations and rarely checked calculations twice.

This semester she negotiated a lower price for fundraiser supplies by agreeing to collect them before closing. Her uncle provided the ride, which she had assumed would be available. She enjoys the back and forth and dislikes designing the advertising sheet. She wants more spending money but sometimes spends her own savings on cousins immediately.

enjoys: Finding inexpensive gifts that feel personal
activities: Watching her brothers three afternoons weekly
demonstratedSkills: Getting adults to discuss prices
Remembering what different buyers care about
Starting conversations with unfamiliar people
unfamiliarActivities: Using a spreadsheet beyond basic entry
Spending a week away from family
motivations: Having enough money to stop postponing household needs
Being useful to relatives
Winning an agreement that initially seemed unlikely
ambitions: Have significant financial comfort as an adult
Take her brothers on a vacation
Explore studying after high school without leaving every family responsibility unresolved
supports: An uncle who sometimes provides rides
A school sponsor who gives direct feedback
practicalConstraints: Uncertain household contributions to further study

biography.selfDescription: I can usually get somebody to talk to me. That doesn't mean I can get every part finished. People forget that distinction.
openQuestions: Would she enjoy keeping records as much as reaching an agreement?
What responsibilities can her family redistribute next year?

biography.name: Nadia Rahman

background.family: Lives with her father, mother, and older sister; family discussions are warm but sometimes lengthy and difficult to exit.
background.finances: Household finances are steady, with money for one paid activity and occasional travel.
background.geography: An apartment neighborhood in Richardson, Texas, near a busy road and a public library.
background.cultureLanguages: English and conversational Bengali at home; observes some family religious traditions while asking questions about others.
background.school: A large public high school where she has a designated quiet place during lunch.
background.accessOpportunities: Her family can provide rides with advance notice. Nadia is autistic; she says clear schedules and quiet recovery time help her participate comfortably.

timeline.story: Nadia liked sitting beside her sister while they filled a shallow tray with water and floated leaves. She disliked getting her sleeves wet and would leave abruptly when cousins splashed. At preschool she wanted the same arrival routine, though her favorite story changed almost every week.

She spent a year collecting pictures of animals from cereal boxes and library discards. When her class voted on a new playground game, she worried about a child who could not run quickly. She suggested letting that child keep time, then learned the child wanted to play too.

An apartment move put the library farther away. Nadia made a calendar showing which days her sister could accompany her. She also tried swimming lessons and disliked the echoing changing room enough to stop. Her parents accepted that decision but continued asking her to try group activities.

She and a neighbor began watering neglected containers outside their building. Some residents liked the flowers; another complained about water on the walkway. Nadia first thought the complaint was unfair. After watching someone slip slightly, she helped move the containers and revised their watering schedule.

She became interested in repairing worn books, practicing on damaged paperbacks rather than library copies. A school discussion about shade outside the entrance stayed with her because students waited there every afternoon. Her first suggestion was too expensive, and she felt embarrassed when a friend pointed that out.

Nadia asked students where they actually waited for rides and recorded their objections to different shade locations. She took written questions to a staff meeting with a friend reading some aloud. She found the discussion tiring, but liked discovering that the bus area had needs she had overlooked.

She is helping a small group revise a proposal for shaded seating. She listens when adults raise supervision and maintenance concerns, although she gets irritated when answers stay vague. Progress is slow. She also reads humorous novels and sometimes ignores group messages for a whole evening because she has had enough conversation.

enjoys: Listening to a specific objection and adjusting a plan
avoids: Being treated as the group's permanent note taker
demonstratedSkills: Collecting different viewpoints
Keeping a discussion tied to a concrete need
Revising a proposal when new facts emerge
motivations: Making ordinary school days less uncomfortable for others
Having objections taken seriously
Seeing a usable result
ambitions: See some seating installed before graduation
Maintain friendships without being available constantly
Experience living somewhere else for a while
struggles: Vague responses feel difficult to interpret
Slow progress makes her doubt the effort
supports: A sister who practices conversations with her
A friend who shares speaking tasks
A staff member who explains practical limits
practicalConstraints: Limited energy after crowded school days
The proposal depends on school decisions

biography.selfDescription: I want people to be able to use the thing we are discussing. Sometimes everybody agrees it is a good idea and somehow nothing happens.
openQuestions: How much continued organizing does she want to take on?
Will she remain interested if only a small version is approved?

biography.name: Evan Liang

background.family: Lives with two parents and a younger sister; grandparents visit for several months most years.
background.finances: Stable middle income; the family budgets deliberately and rarely buys upgrades simply because something newer exists.
background.geography: A suburb north of Houston, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English is easiest for him; he uses limited Mandarin with grandparents and dislikes relatives testing his vocabulary.
background.school: Large public high school where he knows a small circle well and many classmates only by sight.
background.accessOpportunities: Has access to several clubs and reliable family transport, but parents prefer commitments that do not disrupt evenings.

timeline.story: Evan liked building cushions into a tunnel and changing the route after his sister crawled through it. He was quiet around unfamiliar adults and louder at home. At preschool he followed the craft instructions carefully, though he sometimes hid unfinished work because he disliked having it displayed.

He spent months learning a card game from his grandfather and enjoyed remembering which cards had already appeared. Losing could make him sullen. He also liked gardening that year, mainly digging small channels for water, and abandoned it when hot weather made the yard unpleasant after school.

During group projects Evan noticed which classmates wanted to draw and which wanted to present. He quietly offered trades so he could assemble the written parts. A teacher praised his contribution in front of the class, which embarrassed him enough that he avoided volunteering for the next project.

He joined an after-school games group and liked predicting what another player might accept in an exchange. He sometimes waited too long for a better offer and ended with nothing. At home he tried baking bread with his sister but disliked cleaning the sticky mixing bowl afterward.

Two school clubs wanted the same lunch meeting slot. Evan spoke individually with several members and discovered one group mainly wanted access to a particular room. He suggested alternating rooms instead of times. Someone else explained the arrangement publicly, and Evan was relieved to receive little attention.

In a strategy club he became the person who asked what each side would accept when rules or meeting plans were disputed. He preferred private conversations to arguing across a table. Sometimes his compromise avoided the real disagreement, and one friend accused him of caring more about peace than fairness.

Evan helped two clubs divide a shared supply cupboard by asking which materials each actually used. The arrangement worked for several weeks before unlabeled items reappeared. He is willing to revisit the agreement but reluctant to enforce it publicly. Outside school he enjoys cooking simple noodles and watching absurd comedy with his sister.

enjoys: Finding terms both groups can accept
avoids: Enforcing rules in a crowded room
demonstratedSkills: Noticing underlying preferences
Negotiating small practical compromises
Remembering earlier offers and constraints
unfamiliarActivities: Handling a dispute where compromise is impossible
motivations: Having workable arrangements
Being useful without becoming visible
Keeping enough free time
ambitions: Have a room of his own someday
Become more comfortable disagreeing directly
Spend time somewhere his family has never visited
struggles: Sometimes treats quiet as proof a disagreement is resolved
supports: A sister who challenges his evasions
A club advisor who lets him prepare before speaking
practicalConstraints: Does not want every interest to become a commitment

biography.selfDescription: I like figuring out what people would actually agree to. Being the person at the microphone sounds exhausting.
openQuestions: When is he willing to risk an openly unhappy response?
Does he enjoy negotiation when relationships do not become calmer afterward?

biography.name: Brooke Ellison

background.family: Lives with her parents and younger brother; family members are affectionate but compare achievements frequently.
background.finances: Affluent household with extensive travel, new devices, and paid activities readily available.
background.geography: An affluent neighborhood in Austin, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking; family traditions center on vacations, birthdays, and public celebrations of milestones.
background.school: Private secondary school with small classes and many extracurricular options.
background.accessOpportunities: Adults can arrange transport and instruction easily. Brooke often learns about an opportunity through a parent before seeking one herself.

timeline.story: Brooke loved wearing a sparkly dress to family dinners and asking everyone to watch her jump from the lowest stair. She also spent long periods quietly fitting animal puzzles together. When adults stopped watching a performance, she sometimes began again more loudly instead of choosing a different game.

She joined gymnastics after seeing photographs of an older cousin with medals. She liked the matching outfit and learning a cartwheel but complained about repeating basic exercises. A ribbon from a casual school event stayed pinned above her bed much longer than the pictures of the exercises themselves.

Brooke became interested in drawing bedrooms with huge windows and closets. Her mother bought a set of drawing materials, which she used intensely for several weeks. She then moved on to collecting miniature toys. At school she enjoyed reading aloud when she already knew every word in the passage.

She asked to join a demanding activity because successful older students seemed admired. The early sessions involved waiting, practice, and ordinary mistakes, and she soon wanted to stop. Her parents disagreed about whether to insist. She remembers feeling watched by them more than remembering the activity itself.

Brooke started saving photographs of elaborate apartments, expensive trips, and celebration dinners. She said she wanted a life people noticed. She helped at one school sale, but her strongest memory is choosing what to wear; she cannot remember whether taking payments or setting up tables interested her more.

She attended several short programs suggested by adults and liked meeting students from other schools. She described some sessions as inspiring at the time but rarely continued their projects afterward. Her favorite continuing activity was taking long walks with a friend, which she did not consider impressive enough to mention often.

Brooke wants substantial income, a beautiful apartment, and visible recognition in adulthood. When asked what work toward those things she enjoys now, she gives broad answers and changes examples. She recently quit organizing a student event after two meetings. She still reliably helps her brother rehearse presentations when he asks privately.

enjoys: Long walks with one close friend
activities: Keeping an image collection of places and interiors
demonstratedSkills: Giving her brother specific presentation feedback
Describing visual preferences clearly
Making conversation with unfamiliar peers
unfamiliarActivities: Sustaining a self-chosen project for months
motivations: Recognition from peers and family
Financial abundance
Feeling that her life is exceptional
ambitions: Afford an expensive home and frequent travel
Be known for something impressive
Find something she wants to keep doing after praise fades
struggles: Cannot yet identify enduring activity preferences
Compares herself with polished public achievements
supports: A close friend who enjoys ordinary afternoons
A brother who trusts her feedback
practicalConstraints: Little experience making tradeoffs with limited resources
Her schedule contains commitments chosen by adults

biography.selfDescription: I know the kind of life I want. I don't know why everyone expects me to have one favorite thing already.
openQuestions: Which activities would she choose without an audience or award?
What might she continue through an unremarkable middle stage?
How much of her imagined adulthood reflects her own preferences?

biography.name: Elena Vela

background.family: Lives with her father, grandmother, and younger brother; household responsibilities are negotiated day by day.
background.finances: Income fluctuates with available shifts and seasonal repairs. A replacement phone screen is a serious expense.
background.geography: Outside a small town in the Texas Panhandle, beyond the regular town bus route.
background.cultureLanguages: English at school, English and Spanish with her grandmother; understands more Spanish than she confidently speaks.
background.school: Small public school with one mathematics sequence per grade and no advanced mathematics option this year.
background.accessOpportunities: Uses borrowed library books and downloaded pages; home internet sometimes disappears for several days. No competition experience.

timeline.story: Elena arranged bottle caps along the kitchen grout and objected when her brother moved one. Her grandmother remembers a tidy child; Elena remembers wanting to know whether a row could have a middle without having an odd number. Neither account quite replaces the other.

During long drives into town, she invented counting rules for fence posts, sometimes counting only every third post and then restarting. She disliked being asked to demonstrate for visiting adults. At school she liked recess games but argued privately about rules that changed after someone lost.

A library book mentioned a number that could not be written as a fraction. She could follow some examples but not the explanation, and copied a paragraph onto feed-store receipt paper. The paper lived under her mattress until the ink faded; nobody assigned this investigation.

When the family connection stopped working, Elena made paper mazes with restrictions about crossing a line twice. Most failed, and she sometimes tore them up rather than explain the restriction. She also learned to cook eggs for her brother and resented losing uninterrupted afternoons.

She began experiencing persistent anxiety, including a racing heart before ordinary school presentations. A counselor met with her twice before moving away. Mathematics did not cause the anxiety or remove it; she still voluntarily spent evenings wondering which invented rules produced a pattern and which produced a mess.

Elena borrowed an old textbook and skipped between chapters without understanding their sequence. She made a table testing a claim about prime numbers, found an exception, and felt pleased enough to tell her father during dishes. She declined an online contest because connection problems and being timed both bothered her.

She now keeps a notebook labeled Questions Nobody Asked, containing unfinished arguments about infinity alongside grocery totals. Her teacher sometimes checks an argument but has little spare time. Elena wants more difficult material and also wants dependable money, without knowing how extended study could fit the household timetable.

enjoys: Inventing mathematical restrictions and looking for exceptions
Quiet card games with her grandmother
Walking the gravel road at dusk
avoids: Being described as a natural genius
Group chats that require immediate replies
activities: Does occasional paid fence painting with a neighbor
Downloads reading at the town library
demonstratedSkills: Finds counterexamples in her own tables
Explains the difference between a guess and an argument
Keeps younger brother on a workable evening routine
unfamiliarActivities: Sustained work in a large group
motivations: Understanding whether a statement must be true
Having choices without abandoning family obligations
ambitions: Work through a book she currently finds too difficult
Spend several uninterrupted days studying somewhere quiet

biography.selfDescription: “I like the part where an example breaks my rule. I do not like people watching me wait for an idea.”
openQuestions: Would she enjoy sustained formal instruction as much as private puzzles?
Which family responsibilities would remain hers if her schedule changed?
How would she respond to collaborative work without a timer?

biography.name: Graham Sato

background.family: Lives with two parents and an older sister who returns home during breaks; parents are attentive but often plan ahead on his behalf.
background.finances: Household can afford equipment, tutoring, travel, and modifications without delaying other bills.
background.geography: A planned neighborhood north of Dallas, with wide streets and few places reachable without a ride.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; family gatherings include Japanese phrases he recognizes but rarely uses.
background.school: Well-equipped public school with electives, accessible classrooms, and several laboratories.
background.accessOpportunities: Has a powered wheelchair, adjustable desk, laptop, and household tools; some older buildings and outdoor locations remain difficult to access.

timeline.story: Graham watched water travel down the driveway after sprinklers stopped and moved pebbles to alter its route. Adults called the resulting channels artwork, which puzzled him. He wanted to see which puddle emptied first, and rarely cared what the arrangement looked like afterward.

He began using a wheelchair for a mobility impairment and learned that a destination being nearby did not make it reachable. He liked comparing toy ramps with different surfaces. His parents bought elaborate kits, but he returned most often to cardboard, tape, and a kitchen ruler.

Graham measured how far marbles rolled from different starting heights, leaving pencil marks on a strip of masking tape. He disliked a class assignment requiring a decorative poster. He included a plain drawing with measurements and was irritated when neat borders received more discussion than his results.

A family holiday included a museum whose entrance route took much longer than advertised. Graham was angry about missing the first demonstration, then became absorbed in a suspended weight moving across sand. Back home he tried drawing the motion and could not explain several uneven loops.

He learned enough spreadsheet operations to compare repeated measurements of a vibrating ruler. A parent suggested making a video, and he refused because performing an explanation seemed like a separate chore. He enjoyed a small simulation that reproduced only part of the pattern and left the mismatch visible.

His school adjusted a workbench, allowing him to handle materials without another person constantly reaching over him. He liked checking slopes and timing small carts, but skipped an optional art activity and a peer service club. Those invitations were kind; neither felt like something he wanted to repeat.

Graham now draws rough diagrams beside measurements and changes one setting at a time in simple simulations. He has access to demanding courses but is unsure he wants many more years of formal study. His parents hear this as temporary reluctance; he has not decided whether they are right.

avoids: Pitching an idea to a crowd
Activities built mainly around helping strangers
activities: Tests small rolling and swinging objects
Plays strategy games with his sister
demonstratedSkills: Repeats measurements and notices inconsistent runs
Builds readable dimensioned sketches
Makes basic spreadsheet models
unfamiliarActivities: Living away from accessible family housing
motivations: Seeing whether a measured pattern can be explained
Controlling his own schedule and equipment
ambitions: Finish a model that predicts his actual measurements
Try a demanding short course before deciding about longer study
struggles: Adults equate resources with a settled plan
practicalConstraints: Space to position his wheelchair at work surfaces

biography.selfDescription: “I can spend an hour timing something. That does not mean I have agreed to spend ten years studying it.”
openQuestions: Would extended study feel different if he controlled the pace?
Which access arrangements would a new setting actually provide?
Does he enjoy larger shared investigations or mainly his own small models?

biography.name: Mateo Rios

background.family: Lives with his mother, grandfather, and younger sister; adults retain final authority over household spending.
background.finances: Regular but narrow income, with occasional extra expenses that require postponing purchases.
background.geography: El Paso, in a neighborhood with buses to most routine destinations.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English throughout the day; uses whichever makes the exchange simpler.
background.school: Public school with a practical business elective and shared classroom computers.
background.accessOpportunities: Handles limited household records and club supply lists; has no experience negotiating large purchases or supervising others. His grandfather has diabetes, mentioned in family scheduling.

timeline.story: Mateo liked sorting the coins left in a bowl beside the door, then returning them before his mother needed bus fare. He also left toy cars scattered everywhere. Relatives who now call him organized forget that he cared about a few small systems and ignored plenty of others.

At a family picnic he counted juice cartons twice because one cousin had moved a bag. He was irritated by the uncertainty and wrote a small list next time. He did not enjoy handing out the drinks, especially when older children argued that they deserved extra.

His mother let him compare grocery receipts with a handwritten list. He discovered that two similar items had different package sizes, making the cheaper sticker misleading. He liked working out the comparison but became embarrassed when an adult asked him to explain it to everyone in the checkout line.

Mateo helped track borrowed folding chairs after a neighborhood gathering. Three were listed under the wrong household, and he matched a photograph to the original notes to reconcile them. He declined to call the households himself. His uncle interpreted the refusal as shyness, but Mateo mostly disliked asking people for things.

His grandfather’s diabetes meant some appointments had to be worked around bus schedules and family availability. Mateo copied dates into the shared calendar when asked, without becoming responsible for treatment. He grew interested in the trade-offs between saving a fare, spending more time, and missing part of an afternoon.

A school group’s supply money did not match its receipt folder. Mateo found a reimbursement counted twice and a missing cash purchase supported by a dated message. He enjoyed making the record agree. When offered the group’s top position, he declined because persuading members and settling arguments sounded exhausting.

He now compares prices for a few family purchases and keeps a modest personal savings record. He is careful to mark estimates separately from actual amounts. Adults sometimes assume he wants responsibility for all household decisions; he wants to understand the choices without being blamed for choices he cannot make.

enjoys: Reconciling records that do not initially agree
Comparing costs alongside time and inconvenience
Long bus rides with downloaded music
avoids: Being made the final decision maker by default
activities: Occasionally earns money setting up chairs and tables
demonstratedSkills: Separates estimates from actual spending
Checks package quantities before comparing prices
Finds duplicated entries
Explains practical trade-offs in writing
motivations: Knowing where a discrepancy came from
Making a choice understandable before it is made
ambitions: Build a reliable record for his own future expenses
Learn how larger records stay checkable
struggles: People confuse accuracy with willingness to lead

biography.selfDescription: “I can show the options. That is different from promising everybody will like the one they pick.”
openQuestions: Would he enjoy larger records with less personal context?
Can he request missing information without avoiding the whole task?
How much responsibility does he actually want for decisions?

biography.name: Avery Okafor

background.family: Lives with both parents and twin younger siblings; dinner discussions are lively and interruptions are common.
background.finances: Stable middle income, with limits on optional trips and paid summer activities.
background.geography: Fort Worth suburb between newer housing and older industrial streets.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home with some Igbo phrases from extended family; relatives disagree about what counts as a useful pursuit.
background.school: Public school with a library, several advanced classes, and uneven access to teachers after hours.
background.accessOpportunities: Can borrow a laptop and books, visits public lectures online, and has little access to hands-on research spaces.

timeline.story: Avery asked why shadows moved when the furniture stayed still. After an adult explained sunlight, she tested the explanation with a flashlight and her stuffed animals. She lost interest in arranging the animals afterward, but kept asking why two lights sometimes made a less dark patch.

She made up an explanation for why some streets seemed louder than others, based mostly on how close buildings stood. Her father pointed out a quiet narrow lane. Avery argued, then began a new list. She remembers feeling annoyed with him and grateful for the example at different moments.

A library book about time introduced questions she could not settle by looking around the room. Avery reread two pages for several weeks, attaching sticky notes that repeated the same puzzle in slightly different words. She still finished ordinary homework quickly enough to join neighborhood basketball games.

She became convinced that a pattern in bus arrival times reflected a simple cycle. After collecting more examples, she found the cycle depended on which days she had happened to travel. She abandoned the explanation, although she kept a page describing why it had seemed so convincing.

Avery spent a month reading incompatible accounts of how people remember events. She tried explaining one to a friend, who supplied an experience that did not fit. Rather than choose a favorite account, she wrote conditions under which each might fail and became frustrated with her own vague terms.

She returned repeatedly to a theoretical question about how simple local actions can produce a larger pattern. A basic simulation contradicted the explanation she preferred. She changed the rule, then caught herself protecting the original idea and started over. Her unfinished document grew longer while her visible output remained small.

Avery currently cycles between close reading, rough models, and walks where she rehearses an explanation aloud. She likes staying with an idea beyond the week it is assigned. Her parents want a more concrete next step, and she is unsure whether persistent questioning will feel satisfying under fixed deadlines.

enjoys: Revisiting theoretical questions over several weeks
Testing the weak point in an explanation
avoids: Pretending an explanation survived contrary evidence
Choosing a topic solely because it sounds impressive
Packaging unfinished thought as a polished conclusion
activities: Keeps a document of discarded explanations
demonstratedSkills: Identifies assumptions behind a claim
Revises an explanation after contradictory examples
Connects ideas across separate readings
unfamiliarActivities: Sustained practical research in a shared space
Working under tightly managed project deadlines
motivations: Finding a more adequate explanation
Understanding why an initially attractive idea fails
ambitions: Finish one argument with clear limits
Spend time with people willing to examine a question slowly
struggles: Documents expand without reaching an ending
Pressure to make interests visibly useful
supports: Parents make room for reading despite doubts

biography.selfDescription: “I can let an explanation go. It is the question I keep bringing back.”
openQuestions: Will fixed deadlines help her finish or narrow what she enjoys?
How does she respond when collaborators need a provisional decision?
Does she want more practical investigation than she has yet encountered?

biography.name: Elena Ríos

background.family: Lives with her mother, grandmother, and younger brother; her father visits on irregular weekends.
background.finances: Bills usually get paid, but replacement electronics and school trips require saving.
background.geography: An older apartment complex in Garland, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses Spanish with her grandmother and English at school; dislikes being asked to represent either culture.
background.school: Large public high school with crowded classes and a quiet resource room she can use.
background.accessOpportunities: Library internet, a borrowed tablet, and occasional rides from her aunt; few paid activities.

timeline.story: Elena lined up her plastic animals beside the bathtub, then became annoyed when her brother changed the order. She liked telling her grandmother which animals lived in water. She could repeat explanations from television without understanding all their words and sometimes argued when corrected.

Her mother remembers elaborate explanations of card game rules that nobody had requested. Elena liked demonstrating a rule with actual cards but hated deciding who went first. At school she enjoyed picture books about weather and avoided noisy birthday games, even when her friends participated.

After an autism diagnosis, adults discussed accommodations around her more often than she liked. A teacher let her prepare before speaking. Elena explained a rain experiment to a classmate three different ways, then cried when asked to lead the entire table through cleanup.

During remote lessons she made little diagrams for her brother when his fraction homework confused him. Some diagrams were wrong, and she erased them reluctantly after her mother checked. She also spent afternoons watching silly pet videos and left several science kits untouched beneath her bed.

A friend said Elena made everything sound like a lecture. She began asking what part was confusing before drawing examples, although she sometimes forgot to wait for an answer. She liked a small lunch group but declined arranging its movie outing because collecting everyone’s preferences felt exhausting.

She voluntarily helped two classmates understand density by comparing containers from home. When one example failed, she asked the teacher and rewrote it. Her group project went badly when everyone assumed she would allocate tasks. She enjoyed designing the explanation and resented tracking missing contributions.

Elena now shares short annotated examples in a class chat when someone requests help. She likes seeing the point at which another person understands, but repeated interruptions can make her abrupt. She still needs reminders about assignments and has not tried explaining anything regularly to unfamiliar younger children.

enjoys: Finding a second example when the first explanation fails
Subtitled comedy clips with her brother
avoids: Being volunteered to speak without preparation
activities: Shares homework examples with two friends
demonstratedSkills: Notices which step someone missed
Revises examples after checking an error
Remembers details from material she likes
motivations: Wants another person to understand without feeling foolish
Likes having time to prepare
ambitions: Make an explanation booklet that her brother actually uses
Try one optional advanced science class
struggles: Assuming her favorite example is obvious
supports: A teacher who answers follow-up questions
practicalConstraints: Unpredictable visits can change weekend plans

biography.selfDescription: I can explain something well after I have messed up the explanation once. People think that means I want to be in charge, but I do not. I also talk too much sometimes and miss what somebody actually asked.
openQuestions: Would explaining unfamiliar material still be enjoyable?
How much preparation does she need with new people?
Which parts of science interest her beyond helping classmates?

biography.name: Jonah Salazar

background.family: Lives with his parents and two cousins; neither parent attended education beyond high school.
background.finances: Family income varies with hours available, and he shares a bedroom.
background.geography: Outside a small town near Lamesa in West Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home with some Spanish phrases from relatives; family gatherings include several generations.
background.school: Small rural public high school offering few advanced electives.
background.accessOpportunities: County library, school databases, and a long bus ride; travel to larger libraries is rare.

timeline.story: Jonah liked hearing his grandfather tell the same story about a flooded road and interrupted when the details changed. He also liked toy trucks and could spend a whole visit digging outside. His family found the questions funny until he asked them during conversations they wanted to finish.

A school display showed photographs of the town before the highway moved. Jonah wanted to know why some shops disappeared, but mostly copied labels because he did not know how to investigate. He struggled with neat handwriting and lost the short booklet before bringing it home.

He read an old county anniversary book at his aunt’s house and noticed that one family’s account differed from his grandfather’s. Adults offered conflicting explanations. Jonah wrote both down in a spiral notebook, though he also included a rumor without recognizing that it needed checking.

Remote school gave him more reading time and less reliable internet. He compared a newspaper clipping about a school closure with a memoir borrowed from the library. His notes became long and disorganized. He abandoned an online sports club after attending only twice and did not particularly miss it.

An assignment on local water use turned into several evenings reading arguments from different decades. Jonah revised a paragraph after discovering that two writers used the same word differently. He liked the uncertainty, although his final paper arrived late because he kept looking for one more source.

He asked relatives about changes in community celebrations and found that people remembered exclusions differently. He learned to distinguish a personal memory from a claim about everyone. Some relatives thought the topic was unnecessary. He continued reading privately, leaving several promising notes unfinished during a busy harvest season.

Jonah voluntarily spends library afternoons comparing accounts of a nearby settlement’s relocation. He wants time for sustained reading and writing, even if a question takes years to understand. He is the first in his immediate family seriously considering extended study, but costs, distance, and what daily study feels like remain unclear.

enjoys: Long accounts of how communities change
Rewriting an argument when evidence complicates it
avoids: Being rushed to select one simple explanation
activities: Reads county histories and archived newspaper pages
Writes uneven drafts of local questions
demonstratedSkills: Tracks differences between sources
Can sustain reading across several evenings
Revises a claim instead of discarding inconvenient evidence
unfamiliarActivities: Long projects with a formal schedule
motivations: Wants to know why accounts disagree
Finds deep study worthwhile even without an immediate practical result
ambitions: Complete one careful long essay
Learn how to read difficult original documents
Keep studying for several years if he can afford it
supports: One teacher who reads extra drafts
practicalConstraints: Little family familiarity with extended study

biography.selfDescription: I like finding out that a story is more complicated, though that makes me hard to finish with. I do not know whether I am good at studying as a whole. I just know I would keep reading this even without the assignment.
openQuestions: How would he respond to sustained criticism of his writing?
What kind of study setting would be financially reachable?
Would his curiosity extend beyond questions close to home?

biography.name: Tessa Walker

background.family: Stays with an aunt and two cousins while her mother moves between temporary arrangements; contact is frequent but plans change.
background.finances: Little spare money and no stable place to store possessions.
background.geography: Currently near Killeen, Texas, after several moves within the state.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking family; different households have different rules and traditions.
background.school: Third public school in two years, with incomplete activity records.
background.accessOpportunities: School-day opportunities and a phone with intermittent service; no dependable after-school ride or consistently available trusted adult.

timeline.story: Tessa remembers drawing on cereal boxes beside her mother and taking a long time to choose a cartoon. Family photographs suggest she enjoyed playground swings. She does not remember having one favorite activity and becomes uncomfortable when adults expect a clear story about what she has always loved.

She liked eating lunch beside the same two children and making up ridiculous names for their snacks. An after-school dance class was mentioned but never arranged. She sometimes borrowed her cousin’s crayons, although she was more interested in copying a funny face than filling every page.

A move interrupted friendships and changed the bus route. Tessa played simple phone games and watched her cousin braid hair, occasionally trying a braid herself. She declined a school performance because rehearsals required rides, but now cannot separate that practical problem from whether performing would have felt unpleasant.

Remote school was difficult when several people shared devices. She completed some work on paper and missed other lessons. Leisure mostly meant television, walks to a nearby shop, and sending voice messages. She liked choosing music for cleaning but had no equipment or opportunity to try making it.

Tessa helped younger cousins get snacks and sometimes invented a quiet guessing game. She liked them on some afternoons and wanted to be left alone on others. A teacher suggested a club without explaining its meetings. Tessa did not attend and remembers feeling too new to ask basic questions.

Housing changes meant packing possessions into bags twice in one year. She stopped keeping craft materials because carrying them became annoying. At one school she enjoyed a short cooking lesson; at another she avoided signing up because the return transport was unclear. Neither experience tells her much about a lasting preference.

Tessa currently watches comedy clips, walks with a cousin, and sometimes helps prepare rice and eggs. She would like an ordinary week with predictable space and transport. When asked about unfamiliar activities she often says she does not know, then worries that people interpret the answer as refusing to try.

enjoys: Walking to the corner shop with her cousin
avoids: Signing up when transport is uncertain
Keeping supplies she may have to move suddenly

Exchanges voice messages with an old friend

Can prepare a few simple meals
Notices when younger cousins need a quieter activity

Would like chances to try things without a long commitment

Have a small shelf that stays hers

biography.selfDescription: I know what I do after school, but that is mostly what is there. I am tired of picking something on a form when I have never done it. Sometimes I do not want to do anything, and sometimes I would if getting there were simple.
openQuestions: Which activities would she choose with reliable access?
Which preferences persist when housing is settled?
What would a low-pressure first try look like?

biography.name: Avery Nguyen

background.family: Lives with two mothers and an older brother; family conversations are usually supportive.
background.finances: Stable middle income with a budget for selected activities.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home with Vietnamese at some extended family gatherings; they understand familiar phrases.
background.school: Public magnet high school; attendance became uneven during a diagnosed anxiety episode last spring.
background.accessOpportunities: Clubs, a community center, reliable rides, and current support for anxiety; family limits overlapping commitments.

timeline.story: Avery alternated between pretend shops, playground climbing, and coloring with their brother. They usually joined whatever a nearby child suggested. Their mothers remember enthusiasm but disagree about which activity was the favorite, partly because Avery changed the answer depending on who was asking that afternoon.

They liked making paper decorations and playing a simple keyboard borrowed from a cousin. They also enjoyed helping count ingredients for pancakes. A school field game ended in tears after a disagreement over turns, while the next week Avery begged to participate in another outdoor game.

Avery joined a short swimming course and enjoyed practicing a new stroke, although they did not want races. They built a cardboard town for a class display and liked taking photographs on family walks. Finishing and putting everything away were less attractive than starting something with other people.

During remote school they tried bread baking, digital drawing, and learning a song by ear. Some attempts lasted a weekend and others several months. They missed working beside people, but an online group project irritated them because nobody agreed who should decide what the finished thing would look like.

Avery helped with community garden beds, enjoyed a short debate unit, and made a funny video with friends. They liked different parts of each. When asked whether they preferred planning, explaining, making, or organizing, they gave examples for all four and became frustrated at having to choose one.

Last spring anxiety made crowded mornings and uncertain instructions harder, and Avery missed some classes. They still drew at home, practiced a familiar song, and enjoyed quiet baking with their brother. They withdrew from several commitments together, leaving little evidence about whether any particular activity had lost its appeal.

With ongoing support, Avery now attends most school days and has resumed a small garden group. They still enjoy drawing, discussing books, cooking, and casual swimming when energy allows. They cannot yet tell which responsibilities they want repeatedly, and their current limit on commitments feels different from their range of interests.

enjoys: Garden work in a small group
avoids: Too many commitments in one week
activities: Attends a small garden group twice monthly

Can follow and adjust a familiar recipe
Listens and responds in a small discussion
Maintains familiar plant routines

Comparing activities with equal time and access

Wants activities to remain possible while rebuilding stamina

Finish a small illustrated recipe collection
struggles: Current anxiety affects crowded situations and attendance
Finds it difficult to rank enjoyable responsibilities

biography.selfDescription: I can give a real example for almost everything I like. That makes choosing harder. Being anxious changed how much I can do lately, but it did not erase every interest. I also sometimes say yes because the beginning sounds fun and forget about the rest.
openQuestions: Which responsibilities remain appealing after the novelty fades?
What changes as functioning becomes steadier?
How do interests compare when time and access are similar?
